items.prose: Four trades of 1, 2, 3 and 4 lots paid slippage of 2, 4, 9 and 11 bp. A first stump splits at 2.5 lots and predicts the mean on each side.
items.question: What residual is left on the 3-lot trade?

feedback.correct: The right leaf predicts 10 bp, so the residual is −1 bp.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the right leaf's mean, then subtract it from 9.

byKey.flip: You computed $\hat y - y$. The residual is the outcome minus the prediction.
byKey.all: You used the mean of all four trades, 6.5. The stump predicts each side's own mean.

explain.text: The right leaf holds 9 and 11, mean 10. The residual is $y - \hat y = 9 - 10 = -1$. The next stump is fitted to $-1, 1, -1, 1$ on the four trades.

items.prose: Two teams each build 500 trees on the same loan book. Team A grows deep trees on bootstrap samples and averages them. Team B grows depth-2 trees, each fitted to the residuals of the sum so far.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: A mainly cuts variance; B mainly cuts bias, and B's number of trees must be chosen on held-out data
A mainly cuts bias; B mainly cuts variance
options.why: You swapped the two. Averaging deep trees cuts variance; adding small corrections cuts bias.

options.text: Both are random forests with different settings
options.why: B's trees depend on each other: that is boosting, not a forest.

options.text: Adding trees can only help either team
options.why: That holds roughly for A. For B, extra trees eventually fit noise.

feedback.correct: Bagging averages away variance; boosting adds capacity step by step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which team's trees depend on the trees before them.

explain.text: Team A's trees are independent and noisy; their average is steadier. Team B's trees each fix what is left, so the sum grows more flexible, and must be stopped.

items.prose: A model was tuned at ν = 0.2: the validation curve's minimum is at 120 trees. You change to ν = 0.05.
items.question: What should you do about the number of trees?

options.text: Grow well past 120, about 500 or more, and read the new minimum off a fresh validation curve

options.why: You carried the best number of trees across a change of ν. A quarter of the step size needs several times the trees.
Smaller steps need more trees, not fewer.

options.text: It does not matter: small ν never overfits
options.why: Small ν overfits more slowly, but it still overfits, and with too few trees it underfits.

feedback.correct: The best number of trees belongs to one learning rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how far 120 small steps go.

explain.text: At a quarter of the step size, 120 trees cover roughly a quarter of the distance. Search up to 600 or so and let the curve say where it bottoms out.

items.prose: A desk suspects that a carry signal pays only when volatility is low. It boosts stumps on carry and volatility, with ν = 0.05 and 2,000 trees.
items.question: What can this model learn about the suspicion?

options.text: Nothing: stumps add a carry effect and a vol effect, so carry's effect cannot depend on vol

options.why: You expected more trees to help. Any number of stumps is a sum of one-feature steps.

options.text: Half of it, since half the trees will split on vol
options.why: Splitting on vol in one tree and on carry in another still adds two separate effects.

options.text: All of it, if ν is small enough
options.why: ν changes speed, not the shapes the sum can draw.

feedback.correct: Depth 1 is additive; the suspicion is an interaction.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what one split per tree can express.

explain.text: An interaction needs a tree that splits on vol and then on carry. Depth 2 is the least that can do it.

items.prose: A boosted default model currently gives a firm $p = 0.15$. The firm defaulted, $y = 1$.
items.question: What is this firm's target for the next tree under log loss?

widget.label: Next tree target for the firm

feedback.correct: The tree is pushed to raise this firm's log-odds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The target is minus the slope, $y - p$.

byKey.grad: That is the slope itself. The tree fits minus the slope.
byKey.p: That is the current probability, not how far it is from the outcome.

explain.text: The slope of the log loss in the log-odds is $p - y = -0.85$. The tree fits minus that, 0.85, so it raises this firm's log-odds.

items.prose: On 2,000 days of features with 10-day forward labels, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier(early_stopping=True)` stops at 60 trees with a validation log loss well below the base rate's. On the next year it does worse than the base rate.
items.question: What most likely went wrong?

options.text: The random validation fraction held days whose overlapping labels and features had near-copies in training
The market changed in the next year
options.why: It may have, but the validation set had a simpler flaw: it was not later in time.
The test loss is worse than the base rate: more trees would fit more noise.

options.text: The default learning rate is too high
options.why: The learning rate does not explain a validation score that flatters by this much.

feedback.correct: Validate on a later block, with a gap, when labels overlap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which days the validation set held.

explain.text: Each validation day had neighbours in training that share 9 of its 10 label days. The trees memorised them, so stopping came late and the score lied. Pass a later block as validation instead.

items.prose: A direction model scores 55% on 400 walk-forward test days. The base rate, always 'up', is 52%.
items.question: What is its $t$ statistic, to 2 places?

feedback.correct: 1.20 standard errors: not enough on its own.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the 0.03 edge by $\sqrt{b(1 - b)/n}$.

byKey.sd: You divided by the standard deviation of one day, 0.5. Divide by the standard error over 400 days.
byKey.fifty: You measured the edge against 50%. The base rate to beat is 52%.

explain.text: The standard error is $\sqrt{0.2496/400} = 0.025$. So $t = 0.03/0.025 = 1.20$, well short of 2.

items.prose: A model is long £1m on day 1 and short £1m on day 2. The index rises 1.0% on day 1 and falls 0.4% on day 2. Costs are 10 bp per unit traded, starting flat.
items.question: What is the two-day P&L after costs, in £?

widget.label: Two-day P&L in pounds
widget.accept: £11,000: £10,000 + £4,000 gross, less £1,000 to open and £2,000 to flip.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two days' gains, then subtract 10 bp for each unit traded.

byKey.gross: That is before costs. Opening costs £1,000 and the flip trades 2 units, £2,000.
byKey.onecost: You charged the flip as one unit. Long to short is 2 units of £1m.

explain.text: Day 1 gains £10,000 and day 2's short gains £4,000. Opening trades 1 unit (£1,000) and the flip trades 2 (£2,000). Net £11,000.
